findings.text: The first sentence tells a newcomer what Athena is, and the second gives three concrete features. A newcomer can name the project within seconds.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page explains why it is a study of another project instead of an introduction to Athena. That helps, but it is the only argument for why Athena matters. No sentence says what problem Athena solves for the reader or how it compares with other tools.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: The page is Athena's home URL, but its title and nearly all of its body are about firstmate's internals: exit codes, places-held, eleven transition cards and 44 claims. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena must read past a lot of material on a project they did not ask about.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> and the h1 of the same text

findings.text: A link at the top jumps to a clear next-steps list, so a newcomer can find what to do without scrolling through the study. This works well.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" (header) and the Next steps heading

findings.text: The install step starts from a checkout but gives no clone command. It names no prerequisites, such as a Rust toolchain or model API keys, and it does not say what the athena ask command will produce. A newcomer would have to leave for the GitHub repo before they could actually try Athena.
findings.source: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: On Athena's home page, "Start here" points to firstmate, not to Athena. A newcomer could read it as the starting point for Athena itself.
findings.source: Start here heading: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work..."

findings.text: The firstmate summary is plain and defines its terms before using them ("Words used first", Glossary). As an example of Athena's output, the study is readable and shows the claim-tracing that Athena promises.
findings.source: Start here > What firstmate is: "Firstmate is a tool that keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a separate AI coding tool, called a worker..."

findings.text: Some labels and phrases are never explained. The claim tags "mechanism" and "prose-only" do not appear in the Glossary, and "recorded boundary" is internal jargon a stranger cannot decode.
findings.source: Claims and sources: tags "mechanism" and "prose-only"; Limits of this study f1: "The job gave no recorded boundary for running firstmate"

findings.text: This mentions a studies/ folder but does not link to it or say which repository it is in, so a newcomer cannot follow it.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
